label: Acute generalized eruption, with or without fever
q: Is this a benign exanthem or the start of something severe?
lead: This is the presentation where dermatology becomes an emergency specialty. The question is not primarily which rash it is, but whether it is one of the four that kill: SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP with systemic involvement, and meningococcal sepsis. Answer that first.

stop.l: Skin pain out of proportion to what you can see
stop.a: The earliest and most reliable warning of SJS/TEN. Take it seriously before any blister appears. Stop the suspect drug now.

stop.l: Positive Nikolsky sign or epidermal detachment
stop.a: SJS/TEN or staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Burns unit or ICU. Withdraw the culprit drug immediately — shorter half-life drugs carry a better prognosis, so time matters.

stop.l: Mucosal erosions at two or more sites (eyes, mouth, genitals)
stop.a: SJS/TEN. Ophthalmology review within hours — ocular sequelae are the main long-term disability and are largely preventable with early treatment.

stop.l: Facial edema, especially periorbital, with fever and lymphadenopathy
stop.a: DRESS. Check eosinophils, atypical lymphocytes, LFTs, creatinine and TSH. Stop the drug. Expect the hepatitis to persist for weeks after withdrawal.

stop.l: Confluent erythema with skin tenderness and high fever
stop.a: Consider toxic shock syndrome, TEN, or AGEP. Blood cultures, remove any foreign body or packing, and escalate.

stop.l: Non-blanching purpuric lesions with fever and hypotension
stop.a: Meningococcemia or another cause of DIC until disproved. Parenteral antibiotics before imaging or lumbar puncture. Do not wait for the rash to evolve.

stop.l: Fever above 40 °C with palpable purpura, wheeze, or hypotension
stop.a: Systemic severity markers of an adverse cutaneous drug reaction. Admit.

stop.l: Fever with severe headache and an eruption that began on the wrists and ankles
stop.a: Spotted fever rickettsiosis. Start doxycycline now at any age. Serology is negative in the first week, up to 10% never develop a rash, and mortality is driven by treatment delayed past day 5.

dx.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §23 — the most common adverse cutaneous drug reaction
dx.look: Symmetric erythematous macules and papules starting on the trunk and spreading centrifugally, becoming confluent. Onset typically 4–14 days after starting the drug, or within 1–2 days on rechallenge. Pruritic. Mild or no fever. No mucosal erosions.
fr: Symmetric, starts on trunk, spreads outward
ag: Skin pain, Nikolsky sign, epidermal detachment
Two or more mucosal sites eroded
Facial edema, eosinophilia, deranged LFTs
Sterile pustules on erythema
dx.cf: Clinical. The value is in what it excludes: check mucosae, palpate for skin tenderness, and send FBC with differential and LFTs to exclude DRESS.
dx.hp: A superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with occasional eosinophils, mild basal vacuolar change and scattered apoptotic keratinocytes.
dx.assoc: Onset typically 4-14 days after a new drug (sooner on re-exposure). Actively check for the severe-reaction flags - mucosal involvement, facial edema, pustules, organ dysfunction.
dx.mgmt: Stop the culprit drug; supportive care with emollients, topical corticosteroids and antihistamines. Most resolve within 1-2 weeks.

dx.look: Morbilliform or scarlatiniform eruption with prodromal fever, coryza, sore throat or conjunctivitis. Temporal evolution is characteristic: measles spreads head to toe over 3 days; rubella spreads in 24–48 h and clears in the same order.
fr: Prodrome of fever, coryza, conjunctivitis or sore throat
ag: Clear temporal relation to a new high-risk drug
Facial edema with eosinophilia
Mucosal erosions rather than enanthem
dx.cf: Serology or PCR when the specific agent matters for public health (measles, rubella, parvovirus in pregnancy) or when immunosuppressed.
dx.hp: Nonspecific - sparse perivascular lymphocytes with occasional dyskeratotic cells; biopsy rarely helps.
dx.assoc: Identify the agent from context (enterovirus, EBV, parvovirus B19, measles in the unvaccinated); ampicillin during EBV produces a florid morbilliform eruption.
dx.mgmt: Supportive care; the eruption is self-limited. Confirm measles or rubella serology and notify public health where notifiable.

dx.look: Begins 2–8 weeks after starting the drug — later than a simple exanthem. Morbilliform eruption with infiltrated, edematous follicular accentuation, facial edema (especially periorbital), fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytes, and organ involvement, most often hepatitis.
ag: Onset within 3 days of the drug
No systemic features and normal bloods
Sterile pustules dominating
dx.cf: FBC with differential, LFTs, creatinine, urinalysis, TSH now and again at 3 months. Three of: drug eruption, hematologic abnormality, and organ involvement confirms it.
dx.hp: A dense lymphocytic infiltrate, sometimes with atypical lymphocytes and eosinophils, and variable interface change.
dx.assoc: Facial edema, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes and organ involvement (hepatitis, nephritis, myocarditis) 2-8 weeks after the drug; check CBC, LFTs, creatinine and TSH (late thyroiditis). HHV-6 reactivation is common.
dx.mgmt: Stop the culprit immediately and admit; systemic corticosteroids with a slow taper; monitor for organ involvement and delayed thyroid disease.

dx.look: 1–3 weeks after first drug exposure. Prodrome of fever, malaise and arthralgia, then dusky purpuric or target-like macules that coalesce, blister and detach. Mucous membranes invariably involved. Nikolsky positive. SJS <10% detachment, overlap 10–30%, TEN >30%.
fr: Dusky, non-blanching, targetoid macules on trunk
Erosions at two or more mucosal sites
High-risk drug: allopurinol, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, nevirapine, sulfonamides, oxicam NSAIDs
ag: Mucosae entirely normal
Skin non-tender, Nikolsky negative
Sterile pustules without necrosis
dx.cf: Clinical, urgently. Frozen-section or punch biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis and confirms within the hour when the diagnosis is disputed. Calculate SCORTEN for prognosis and triage.
dx.hp: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal detachment and a sparse dermal infiltrate - confirms it and separates it from staphylococcal scalded skin (a subcorneal split).
dx.assoc: Almost always drug-induced (aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, nevirapine); calculate SCORTEN, involve ophthalmology early, and consider HLA-B typing in at-risk groups.
dx.mgmt: Immediate withdrawal of the culprit; burns-unit or ICU supportive care; early ophthalmology. Adjuvant cyclosporine, etanercept or IVIG is used per local protocol.

dx.look: Rapid onset, usually within 1–4 days of the drug — faster than any other severe reaction. Dozens to hundreds of small non-follicular sterile pustules on edematous erythema, starting in the flexures and face. Fever and neutrophilia. Resolves with superficial desquamation in about 2 weeks.
fr: Onset within 1–4 days of the drug
Sheets of pinhead non-follicular sterile pustules
ag: Latency of weeks
Personal or family history of psoriasis (points to pustular psoriasis instead)
Mucosal erosions
dx.cf: Biopsy shows subcorneal or intraepidermal spongiform pustules with papillary dermal edema and eosinophils. Pustule swab is sterile — that is the point.
dx.hp: Subcorneal and intraepidermal spongiform pustules with papillary dermal edema and often eosinophils - the eosinophils and necrotic keratinocytes help separate it from pustular psoriasis.
dx.assoc: Onset within days of the culprit (aminopenicillins, macrolides, diltiazem, hydroxychloroquine); neutrophilia is expected. Check calcium and renal function if extensive.
dx.mgmt: Stop the drug; supportive care with topical corticosteroids. Self-limited, resolving with desquamation over 1-2 weeks.

dx.look: Sheets of sterile pustules on fiery erythema with high fever, in a patient who usually has a personal or family history of psoriasis, or who has just had systemic steroids withdrawn. Hypocalcemia and hypoalbuminemia are characteristic.
fr: Known psoriasis, or recent systemic steroid withdrawal
ag: Clear single-drug trigger with 1–4 day latency
No psoriasis history and no nail or joint signs
dx.cf: Biopsy shows spongiform pustules of Kogoj on a psoriasiform background. Check calcium, albumin and renal function — these drive the acute risk.
dx.hp: Spongiform pustules of Kogoj with subcorneal neutrophils on a psoriasiform background.
dx.assoc: An emergency - waves of sterile pustules with fever and leukocytosis; check calcium, albumin and renal function, and look for a trigger (steroid withdrawal, infection, pregnancy - impetigo herpetiformis). IL36RN mutations occur in some.
dx.mgmt: Admit for supportive care and fluids; acitretin, cyclosporine, methotrexate or infliximab for rapid control; the IL-36 inhibitor spesolimab is now used for flares.

dx.look: Diffuse blanching sandpaper erythema with accentuation in the flexures (Pastia lines), strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor, and late desquamation of palms and soles. Toxic shock adds hypotension and multiorgan involvement. SSSS in young children gives superficial peeling with a positive Nikolsky but no mucosal involvement.
fr: Late desquamation of hands and feet
Hypotension with multiorgan involvement suggests TSS
ag: Clear drug latency with pruritus and no toxicity
Mucosal erosions with epidermal detachment on the trunk
dx.cf: Throat swab and culture, ASO titer, blood cultures. In suspected TSS, look for and remove the source: tampon, packing, surgical wound.
dx.hp: Biopsy is not part of the diagnosis - the decision rests on the clinical picture, cultures and source control. If a specimen is taken, staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome shows a subcorneal split through the granular layer with acantholysis and almost no inflammation or organisms, while scarlet fever and toxic shock show only dermal edema with a sparse perivascular infiltrate.
dx.assoc: Identify the source - group A streptococcus (scarlet fever), or Staphylococcus aureus (toxic shock, scalded skin); toxic shock demands a search for retained tampon or packing plus blood cultures.
dx.mgmt: Antistreptococcal or antistaphylococcal antibiotics, source control and fluids; escalate toxic shock syndrome to critical care.

dx.look: Non-pruritic coppery papulosquamous eruption involving palms and soles, with generalized lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms. Can closely mimic a drug exanthem and is regularly missed for exactly that reason.
ag: Intense pruritus with clear drug timing
Sparing of palms and soles
dx.cf: Treponemal test with RPR titer. Offer HIV testing.
dx.hp: A psoriasiform and lichenoid dermatitis with a plasma-cell-rich infiltrate and endothelial swelling; spirochetes are shown on Warthin-Starry stain or immunohistochemistry.
dx.assoc: A marker of HIV risk - offer HIV testing to everyone diagnosed; screen for other sexually transmitted infections and notify partners.
dx.mgmt: Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly for early syphilis; doxycycline if penicillin-allergic and not pregnant. Report to public health and trace contacts.

dx.look: In a transplant recipient, typically 2–6 weeks post-engraftment: erythema starting on the palms, soles, ears and upper trunk, with follicular accentuation, progressing to a morbilliform or, at its worst, a TEN-like eruption. Diarrhea and cholestatic liver derangement accompany it.
fr: Allogeneic stem cell or solid organ transplant
Acral and ear onset with follicular accentuation
ag: No allogeneic stem cell, marrow or organ transplant
Onset beyond 100 days with lichenoid or sclerodermoid change
Palms, soles and ears spared, with no pain on pressure
dx.cf: Biopsy with clinical grading. Coordinate with the transplant team — the skin is one organ in a multiorgan diagnosis.
dx.hp: Basal vacuolar interface change with apoptotic keratinocytes and satellite lymphocytes (satellite-cell necrosis); graded by severity.
dx.assoc: Two to six weeks after allogeneic transplant, a morbilliform eruption favoring the palms, soles and ears, often with hepatic and gastrointestinal involvement; the differential is drug and viral eruptions.
dx.mgmt: Topical corticosteroids for limited skin disease; systemic corticosteroids first-line for significant or multi-organ acute GVHD, directed by the transplant team.

dx.look: A child under 5 with fever for 5 or more days plus at least four of: bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection, oral mucosal change (cracked lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphous rash, extremity change (erythema then periungual desquamation), and cervical lymphadenopathy over 1.5 cm.
fr: Perineal accentuation of rash, later periungual peeling
ag: Age over 8
Fever resolving within 3 days
dx.cf: Echocardiography for coronary artery aneurysm, plus CRP, ESR, platelets, albumin and LFTs. This is a clinical diagnosis with a time-critical treatment window — IVIG within 10 days of fever onset.
dx.hp: Biopsy has no role - this is a clinical diagnosis made against the fever and mucocutaneous criteria, with echocardiography as the investigation that matters. Acute-phase skin shows endothelial swelling in postcapillary venules, dilated dermal vessels and a perivascular lymphocytic and monocytic infiltrate around dermal arterioles.
dx.assoc: Fever for 5 or more days with conjunctival injection, mucosal changes, extremity changes, rash and cervical lymphadenopathy; the danger is coronary artery aneurysm - obtain an echocardiogram.
dx.mgmt: IVIG plus aspirin, ideally within 10 days of fever onset; urgent pediatric and cardiology referral.

dx.look: Bilateral, symmetric, acrally predominant target lesions - a dull red or blistering center, a pale edematous ring, and an outer red rim - on the dorsal hands, palms, forearms, elbows and knees, evolving over about 10 days. EM minor spares the mucosae; EM major always involves them and is more often drug-related.
fr: True three-zone target lesions with a dusky or blistering center
Acral predominance on dorsal hands, palms, forearms, elbows and knees
Cold sore or genital herpes several days before onset
Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection in a child or young adult
ag: Truncal onset with confluent dusky macules and skin pain
Detachment of more than 10% of the body surface
Long drug latency with facial edema and eosinophilia
dx.cf: Clinical. Biopsy shows interface dermatitis with keratinocyte apoptosis and a subepidermal split, and immunofluorescence is negative. The call that matters is separating EM from early SJS: EM is acral with well-formed targets, SJS is truncal with flat atypical targets and skin pain.
dx.hp: Perivascular mononuclear infiltrate with upper dermal edema, apoptotic keratinocytes and focal epidermal necrosis with subepidermal blistering; severe cases show full-thickness necrosis indistinguishable from toxic epidermal necrolysis.
dx.assoc: Most cases follow herpes simplex; Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the other common trigger and produces mucosa-predominant disease in children. Sulfonamides, phenytoin, barbiturates, penicillin and allopurinol are the recognized drug triggers. Ocular involvement can progress to keratitis and corneal ulceration.
dx.mgmt: Treat or suppress the trigger - an antiviral for HSV-associated disease with continuous suppression to prevent recurrence, a macrolide for Mycoplasma. Symptomatic topical corticosteroids and antiseptic mouthwash; admit EM major for fluids, mucosal care and ophthalmology review.
dx.pat: Acral targets, dorsal hands and palms

dx.n: Acute HIV seroconversion illness (acute retroviral syndrome)
dx.look: Three to four weeks after exposure: fever, pharyngitis, tender lymphadenopathy, headache and myalgia, with an exanthem appearing 2 to 3 days after the fever and lasting 5 to 8 days - discrete pink macules and papules up to 1 cm on the upper thorax, collar region, face and arms that stay discrete rather than becoming confluent. Aphthous-like ulcers of the palate, tonsils, genitals or anal canal are the giveaway.
fr: Fever, pharyngitis and tender lymphadenopathy 2 to 4 weeks after exposure
Discrete, non-confluent pink macules and papules on the upper trunk, collar region and face
Painful aphthous-like ulcers on palate, tonsils, genitals or anal canal
Headache or retro-orbital pain, myalgia, diarrhea and weight loss
Sexual or injection exposure in the preceding month
No new drug that accounts for the eruption
ag: Clear temporal relation to a new high-risk drug with eosinophilia
Confluent eruption with pruritus dominating
No mucosal ulceration and no exposure history
dx.cf: HIV RNA viral load or a fourth-generation antigen/antibody assay. Antibody-only testing is negative in the window period, which is exactly when this syndrome presents. Repeat serology at 6 weeks to document seroconversion.
dx.hp: Nonspecific - a sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes. The diagnosis is virologic, not histologic.
dx.assoc: Up to 70% of primary HIV infections are symptomatic. Mean duration of illness is about 13 days, and prolonged symptomatic primary infection predicts a more rapid decline in immune function. Screen for other sexually transmitted infections.
dx.mgmt: Refer immediately for antiretroviral therapy - treating in acute infection is standard and improves outcomes. Notify partners, screen for other STIs, and counsel on transmission risk, which is at its highest during this high-viremia phase.

dx.look: Abrupt fever, rigors, severe headache, myalgia and prostration in a previously well child or young adult. Small pink blanchable macules and papules appear early and become petechial within hours - ankles, wrists, axillae, conjunctivae and palate first - then ecchymoses, hemorrhagic bullae and map-like gray-black infarcts as disseminated intravascular coagulation sets in.
fr: Non-blanching petechiae or purpura in a febrile, ill-looking patient
Rash evolving over hours rather than days
Petechiae at pressure points and on the conjunctivae and palate
Hypotension, cold hands and feet, mottling, severe leg pain
Adolescent or young adult, crowded living, asplenia or complement deficiency
ag: Systemically well with normal observations
Blanching pruritic eruption evolving over days
No fever
dx.cf: Do not wait for confirmation. Blood cultures and meningococcal PCR, with lumbar puncture when it is safe - but parenteral antibiotics go in first. A scraping or aspirate from a purpuric lesion can show gram-negative diplococci within minutes.
dx.hp: Thrombosis of dermal vessels with neutrophilic infiltration, hemorrhage and epidermal necrosis; organisms may be visible in vessel walls on Gram stain.
dx.assoc: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is fulminant septicemia with widespread purpura, DIC, thrombocytopenia and adrenal failure. Survivors may need amputation for peripheral gangrene. Notify public health the same day and arrange prophylaxis for close contacts.
dx.mgmt: Immediate parenteral ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin before transfer, imaging or lumbar puncture; fluid resuscitation and critical care. Notify public health and give contact chemoprophylaxis.

dx.n: Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other spotted fever rickettsioses
dx.look: Abrupt fever, rigors, severe headache, myalgia, nausea and vomiting, with 2 to 6 mm pink blanchable macules appearing around day 3 on the wrists, forearms and ankles and spreading centripetally to trunk and face within 6 to 18 hours, involving the palms and soles. Over 2 to 4 days the lesions become deep red papules and then non-blanching petechiae.
fr: Rash begins on the wrists and ankles and spreads centripetally
Tick exposure or outdoor activity in an endemic area, usually spring or summer
Severe headache, myalgia and vomiting preceding the rash
ag: Eruption starting on the trunk and spreading outward
Systemically well with no fever
Midwinter onset with no outdoor exposure
dx.cf: Treat empirically on clinical and epidemiologic grounds. Serology is negative in the first week and confirmation is retrospective on paired sera. Only 3% present with the triad of rash, fever and known tick bite in the first 3 days, and about 40% never recall a bite.
dx.hp: Lymphohistiocytic vasculitis of small dermal vessels with endothelial swelling, fibrin thrombi and extravasated erythrocytes; immunohistochemistry on a punch biopsy of a purpuric lesion can demonstrate rickettsiae rapidly.
dx.assoc: Rickettsia rickettsii, transmitted by dog and wood ticks. Up to 10% are spotless, and that group carries the higher mortality because the diagnosis is delayed. Diabetes, cardiac insufficiency and alcohol use worsen outcome.
dx.mgmt: Doxycycline immediately in anyone suspected, at any age including young children - delay beyond day 5 of illness is the main determinant of death. Do not wait for serology and do not substitute a beta-lactam.

dx.n: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema (SDRIFE)
dx.look: Sharply demarcated V-shaped erythema of the gluteal, perianal and inguinal skin with symmetric involvement of at least one other flexure - axillae, antecubital or popliteal fossae - beginning hours to days after a systemic drug, most often an aminopenicillin. No fever, no mucosal involvement, and the person looks well.
fr: Sharply demarcated V-shaped erythema of buttocks, perianal skin and groin
Symmetric involvement of at least one other flexure
Onset within hours to days of a systemic drug, commonly an aminopenicillin
Systemically well - no fever and normal observations
No prior topical exposure to the same agent
ag: Fever with neutrophilia and sheets of sterile pustules
Mucosal erosions
Widespread truncal eruption that spares the folds
dx.cf: Clinical, on distribution plus drug timing. Delayed-reading patch or intradermal testing after resolution supports it. The separation that matters is from AGEP, which shares the flexural onset but adds fever, neutrophilia and sheets of pustules.
dx.hp: Superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with mild spongiosis and scattered eosinophils and neutrophils - nonspecific, and used mainly to exclude AGEP.
dx.assoc: Aminopenicillins are the commonest trigger, followed by other beta-lactams, chemotherapeutic agents, iodinated contrast and biologics. This is systemic delayed hypersensitivity, not contact allergy, so no prior topical exposure is needed.
dx.mgmt: Stop the drug and document the reaction; topical corticosteroids and emollients. Resolves over 1 to 2 weeks, sometimes with desquamation.

dx.look: Quotidian fever spiking above 39 °C in the late afternoon or evening, with an evanescent salmon-pink macular eruption on the trunk and proximal limbs that appears at the fever spike and has gone by morning. Arthralgia or frank arthritis, sore throat, and a strikingly high ferritin.
fr: Fever spiking once daily, usually in the evening, with the rash appearing at the spike
Evanescent salmon-pink macules that fade within hours
Arthralgia or arthritis with sore throat
Ferritin many times the upper limit of normal
Neutrophilic leukocytosis with negative ANA and rheumatoid factor
ag: Fixed eruption that persists between fever spikes
Clear culprit drug with eosinophilia and hepatitis
High-titer ANA with organ-specific autoimmunity
dx.cf: A diagnosis of exclusion: quotidian fever, arthralgia, the typical rash and leukocytosis, plus sore throat, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or abnormal liver tests, after infection, malignancy and other rheumatic disease have been excluded. Ferritin and blood cultures are the first tests.
dx.hp: Sparse superficial perivascular and interstitial neutrophilic infiltrate with scattered dyskeratotic keratinocytes in the upper epidermis - a helpful pattern when it is present.
dx.assoc: Watch for macrophage activation syndrome: falling cell counts, a falling ESR with rising ferritin and triglycerides, and liver failure. Persistent pruritic brown plaques mark a more severe course.
dx.mgmt: NSAIDs for mild disease; systemic corticosteroids for most, with methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent and IL-1 or IL-6 blockade for refractory disease. Rheumatology referral.

ctx.l: A new drug started in the last 8 weeks
Onset within 1–4 days of the drug
ctx.s: AGEP has the shortest latency of the severe reactions, Fitzpatrick 8e §23
DRESS latency is characteristically long, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

ctx.l: High-risk drug (allopurinol, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, sulfonamide, nevirapine)
ctx.s: EuroSCAR / RegiSCAR case-control data on high-risk drugs

ctx.l: Sick contacts or a community outbreak
Known psoriasis, or systemic steroid recently withdrawn

ctx.s: HIV/AIDS is a recognized risk factor for SJS/TEN, Fitzpatrick 8e §8

ctx.l: Tick exposure or outdoor activity in an endemic area
ctx.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25 - only about 60% of RMSF cases recall a tick bite

ctx.l: Sexual or injection exposure in the last 3 months
ctx.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §27,§30 - acute retroviral syndrome presents 2 to 4 weeks after exposure

find.l: Skin pain or tenderness disproportionate to the visible rash
find.s: Listed first among findings indicating a life-threatening ACDR, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Positive Nikolsky sign or frank epidermal detachment
Erosions at two or more mucosal sites
find.s: Mucous membranes are invariably involved in SJS/TEN, Fitzpatrick 8e §8

find.l: Dusky, non-blanching targetoid macules coalescing on the trunk
Facial edema, especially periorbital
find.s: Facial edema is characteristic of DRESS, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Eosinophilia ≥1500/µL or atypical lymphocytes
find.s: A proposed diagnostic criterion for DRESS, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Transaminases at least twice the upper limit of normal
find.s: Hepatitis is the commonest organ involvement in DRESS, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Tender generalized lymphadenopathy
Sheets of small non-follicular sterile pustules on erythema
Flexural and facial onset of the pustular eruption
find.s: AGEP characteristically begins in the flexures, Fitzpatrick 8e §23

find.l: Neutrophilia with fever
Prodromal coryza, conjunctivitis or sore throat
Palms and soles involved
Marked pruritus
Sandpaper texture with flexural accentuation (Pastia lines)
Strawberry tongue
Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection
Fever persisting 5 days or more despite antibiotics
Diarrhea with rising bilirubin in a transplant recipient
Patient looks systemically well, normal observations
find.s: Systemic wellness is the strongest single argument against a severe cutaneous adverse reaction

find.l: Well-formed three-zone target lesions with a dusky or blistering center
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - iris or target lesions are typical of erythema multiforme

find.l: Acral predominance on dorsal hands, forearms, elbows and knees
Cold sore or genital herpes several days before the eruption
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - most erythema multiforme follows herpes simplex

find.l: Painful aphthous-like ulcers on palate, tonsils or genitals with the exanthem
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §27 - aphthous-type ulcers of acute HIV syndrome

find.l: Discrete non-confluent pink macules and papules on the upper trunk and collar region
Non-blanching petechiae or purpura appearing within hours in a febrile patient
Hypotension, cold extremities or delayed capillary refill
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25 - meningococcal septicemia and toxic shock syndrome

find.l: Neck stiffness, photophobia or altered consciousness
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25,§27 - CNS involvement is common in RMSF and meningococcal disease

find.l: Eruption began on the wrists and ankles and spread centripetally
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25 - RMSF is the spotted fever that begins distally

find.l: Salmon-pink eruption that appears with the daily fever spike and fades by morning
Ferritin many times the upper limit of normal
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - calibrated estimate, the direction is certain

find.l: Sharply demarcated V-shaped erythema of buttocks and groin with another flexure involved
Eruption confined to the flexures with no fever and no mucosal involvement

test.l: FBC with differential, LFTs, creatinine, urinalysis
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §23 — proposed diagnostic criteria for drug hypersensitivity syndrome
test.w: On every generalized drug-associated eruption, not only the ones that look severe. This panel is what separates a simple exanthem from DRESS, and the two look identical on day one.
test.p: Eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytes with organ derangement makes DRESS. Stop the drug, and be prepared for the hepatitis to run on for weeks after withdrawal.
test.n: Normal bloods in a well patient support a simple exanthematous eruption. Repeat at one week if the rash progresses or fever develops — DRESS declares itself late.
test.x: Check TSH at diagnosis and again at 3 months. Autoimmune thyroiditis is a well-described delayed sequela of DRESS and is missed because nobody looks for it.

test.l: Lesional skin biopsy, frozen section if urgent
test.w: When epidermal necrolysis is suspected and the diagnosis is disputed, or when staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome must be separated from TEN in a child.
test.p: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate and a subepidermal split confirms TEN. In SSSS the split is subcorneal instead — the level of the split is the whole answer.
test.n: Does not exclude very early disease sampled before necrosis is established. Re-biopsy if the clinical course progresses.
test.x: Immunofluorescence is unremarkable in SJS/TEN, which is useful: it rules out the autoimmune blistering diseases in the same specimen. Send a second piece in Michel medium.

test.l: Biopsy for spongiform pustules; swab the pustules
test.w: Any acute generalized pustular eruption — to separate AGEP from generalized pustular psoriasis and from infection.
test.p: Subcorneal or intraepidermal spongiform pustules with papillary edema and dermal eosinophils favors AGEP. A sterile pustule swab supports it.
test.n: Histology overlaps substantially with pustular psoriasis. The drug latency and the psoriasis history usually decide it, not the slide.
test.x: Eosinophils in the infiltrate and marked papillary edema favor AGEP; a psoriasiform epidermis with tortuous capillaries favors pustular psoriasis. Neither is decisive alone.

test.w: Any generalized eruption involving palms and soles, and any generalized eruption without a clear drug or viral cause.
test.p: Stage, treat with benzathine penicillin G, notify partners, and offer HIV testing.
test.n: A negative treponemal test excludes secondary syphilis.
test.x: Ask for dilution if the clinical picture is convincing and the RPR is low — the prozone phenomenon produces false negatives at very high antibody titers.

test.l: Blood cultures with throat swab and ASO titer
test.w: Fever with confluent blanching erythema, especially with a sandpaper texture or strawberry tongue, and in anyone hypotensive.
test.p: Confirms the streptococcal or staphylococcal source. In toxic shock, find and remove the focus — tampon, packing, surgical wound.
test.n: Blood cultures are often negative in toxin-mediated disease because the toxin, not bacteremia, drives the illness. A negative culture does not exclude toxic shock.
test.x: Do not delay antibiotics for culture results in a hypotensive patient.

test.l: Echocardiography with CRP, ESR, platelets, albumin
test.w: Any child under 5 with unremitting fever for 5 days plus mucocutaneous findings. Do not wait for all five criteria — incomplete Kawasaki disease is common and carries the same coronary risk.
test.p: Coronary dilatation or aneurysm confirms and dictates urgent IVIG plus aspirin.
test.n: A normal early echo does not exclude Kawasaki disease. Aneurysms typically appear in the second to third week. Repeat at 2 and 6 weeks.
test.x: The treatment window that protects the coronaries is within 10 days of fever onset. Treat on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for imaging to declare itself.

test.l: HIV RNA viral load with a fourth-generation antigen/antibody assay
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §27 - detection of HIV RNA and antigen, with demonstrated seroconversion
test.w: Any acute generalized eruption with fever, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy that no drug or common virus explains, and in anyone with an exposure history or mucosal ulceration.
test.p: A high viral load with negative or indeterminate antibody is acute HIV infection. Refer the same week for antiretroviral therapy, notify partners, and screen for other sexually transmitted infections.
test.n: A negative antibody test alone does not exclude it - that is the window period, and it is precisely when this syndrome occurs. Send RNA or an antigen assay and repeat serology at 6 weeks.
test.x: Ordering antibody-only testing is the classic error. A low-level positive RNA result should be repeated before it is acted on.

test.l: Blood cultures and meningococcal PCR, taken after the first dose of antibiotic
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25 - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Any febrile patient with non-blanching lesions, and any febrile, ill-looking patient whose eruption is evolving over hours whatever its current morphology.
test.p: Confirms meningococcal disease. Continue ceftriaxone, notify public health the same day, and arrange chemoprophylaxis for close contacts.
test.n: A negative culture after antibiotics does not exclude it. PCR stays positive for days and is the test that survives pretreatment - treat on clinical grounds regardless.
test.x: Antibiotics come first. Delaying the first dose for cultures, imaging or lumbar puncture is what kills. A scraping or aspirate of a purpuric lesion can show gram-negative diplococci within minutes.

test.l: Empiric doxycycline with paired acute and convalescent rickettsial serology
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §25 - clinical and epidemiologic considerations outweigh laboratory diagnosis early; accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Fever, severe headache and an eruption starting on the wrists and ankles in anyone with plausible tick exposure. Start treatment at the point of suspicion.
test.p: A fourfold rise in titer between acute and convalescent sera confirms it retrospectively. Complete the doxycycline course regardless of when the result arrives.
test.n: First-week serology is negative in most cases and must never be used to withhold doxycycline. Immunohistochemistry on a punch biopsy of a purpuric lesion is the only rapid confirmatory test.
test.x: Waiting for confirmation is the commonest fatal error here. Doxycycline is the drug of choice at every age, including in young children, where tooth staining is not a reason to withhold it.

test.l: Lesional biopsy to separate erythema multiforme from early epidermal necrolysis
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Target-like lesions that are blistering or becoming confluent, any truncal spread, or any eroded mucosal surface.
test.p: Interface dermatitis with apoptotic keratinocytes and a subepidermal split supports erythema multiforme, and negative immunofluorescence on the same specimen excludes the autoimmune blistering diseases.
test.n: Histology cannot reliably separate EM major from SJS. That call is clinical: acral true targets are EM, truncal flat atypical targets with skin pain are SJS.
test.x: Never let a biopsy delay drug withdrawal. If SJS is a serious possibility, stop the suspect drug now and manage as necrolysis while the specimen is processed.

test.l: Ferritin with blood cultures and an infection and malignancy screen
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Daily fever spikes with an evanescent rash and arthralgia in a young adult, once a drug cause has been considered and excluded.
test.p: A markedly raised ferritin with neutrophilic leukocytosis and negative ANA and rheumatoid factor supports adult-onset Still disease. Refer to rheumatology.
test.n: A normal ferritin makes it unlikely and should push you back toward infection, lymphoma or a drug reaction.
test.x: This is a diagnosis of exclusion - blood cultures, echocardiography and imaging for lymphoma come first. A falling ESR with rising ferritin and falling cell counts signals macrophage activation syndrome, which is an emergency.

test.l: Drug timeline with delayed-reading patch testing after resolution
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Symmetric flexural erythema beginning within days of a systemic drug in someone who is otherwise well.
test.p: A positive delayed patch or intradermal reaction supports the diagnosis and documents the allergy for future prescribing.
test.n: Patch testing is negative in many genuine cases. A convincing timeline with the characteristic distribution is enough to record the drug as the cause.
test.x: Test at least 6 weeks after the eruption has cleared. Do not mistake this for AGEP - fever, neutrophilia and sterile pustules move both the diagnosis and the risk category.

flag: Drug eruptions can mimic virtually every morphologic pattern in dermatology and must be the first consideration in any suddenly appearing eruption (Fitzpatrick 8e §23). Before you settle on a benign label, actively look for the six severity markers: skin pain, facial edema, mucosal erosion, Nikolsky sign, palpable purpura, and fever above 40 °C.
